transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-03
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (CTO, EdgeFlux), Tom Nguyen (Platform Eng), Sara Brooks (Sec Lead)

Summary:
EdgeFlux is evaluating Redwood Dedicated for predictable reserved GPU capacity. Primary concerns: blast-radius/isolation between tenants, burst behavior (hot pool prewarm vs cold starts), failover SLAs across regions, and encrypted KMS/HSM integration for keys. They want concrete sizing guidance for reserved nodes and example fallback playbooks if Dedicated capacity saturates. Next: Redwood to provide pricing matrix and topology sketch; customer to provide traffic profile.

Topics covered:
- Current infra and multi-tenant patterns
- Peak vs baseline token qps and scaling expectations
- Isolation strategies (node fencing, tenant sharding, soft quotas)
- Prewarm/warmpool behavior and cost tradeoffs
- Failover patterns (fallback to hosted variants / regional burst)
- Security and compliance (KMS, audit logs, SSO/SAML)

Action items (captured above)

Transcript body:
[00:00:02] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Priya, Tom, Sara — thanks for joining. We're here to go through EdgeFlux's reserved capacity needs and talk through isolation and burst. Can you start with context on workload?

[00:00:18] Priya Patel: Yeah, sure. So quick background: EdgeFlux is building an agent orchestration layer for real-time support and automated risk signals. We have steady baseline inference — around 800 requests per minute for embeddings and classification — but we get sharp season spikes when clients push campaigns, 10x for like 5 to 20 minutes.

[00:00:35] Tom Nguyen: To add — some requests are long context generation, e.g., 2k token incr, which hits GPU memory and KV cache. We need predictable throughput and also isolation — we don't want a noisy tenant to push us into OOMs.

[00:00:52] Luis Ortega: Got it. When you say KV cache, do you mean prefix caching across request patterns or per-tenant key value cache?

[00:00:58] Tom Nguyen: Per-tenant mostly, we store session KV across long chats. Also, we have strict p95/p99 SLAs for some customers.

[00:01:06] Sara Brooks: On the security side — we need KMS integration (customer-managed keys), audit logs for inference requests stored 1 year, and SAML SSO. Also wondering about data residency — some EU customers must keep embeddings in-region.

[00:01:20] Maya Chen: Totally. Those are all on our checklist — Redwood Private covers the full KMS/HSM integration, Dedicated supports CMK via endpoint integration and audit logs shipped to your SIEM. We'll detail retention options in the security docs.

[00:01:35] Priya Patel: The main question is capacity: do we reserve nodes equal to 2x baseline and rely on burst options, or is it better to reserve for peak? Cost matters. We want guidance on blast-radius if we shard tenants across nodes.

[00:01:47] Luis Ortega: Good question. Typical pattern: reserve baseline plus a warm pool for burst. Reserved nodes give predictable throughput for baseline; warm pool (prewarmed GPUs) is cheaper than over-reserving peak. The tradeoff is that warm pool can be preempted in multi-tenant clouds unless you choose Dedicated hot-pool isolation.

[00:02:05] Tom Nguyen: How deterministic is the prewarm timing? If we spin up a warm pod, how long until it's fully useful for KV-heavy generative workloads?

[00:02:12] Luis Ortega: For medium-sized LLMs with KV cache warmup, expect 20–45 seconds to reach steady-state for the model KV buffers. For very large sequences it can be 60s+. We also do prefix caching to mitigate. There is some variability — and in the transcript you might see the term K V cash in our notes, that's the transcriber messing up KV cache.

[00:02:30] Priya Patel: Ok, that matters — clients expect sub-500ms token latency for streaming. We can't tolerate 60s cold.

[00:02:35] Maya Chen: Understood. Two levers: (1) keep a hot pool sized to cover your 95th percentile burst size so streaming latency stays low; (2) route non-latency-critical jobs to lower-cost hosted models or quantized variants. We can recommend quantization profiles if you want to shave cost.

[00:02:52] Sara Brooks: If we do hot pools, what about blast-radius? If a tenant spikes, can they exhaust a whole node and affect other tenants?

[00:02:58] Luis Ortega: Node-level isolation options: tenant fencing (pin tenants to dedicated lanes), soft quotas with circuit breaker policies, and tenant-sharding so high-risk tenants get their own reserved slices. We also support preemptive throttles that eject requests once a tenant breaches the quota, preventing full node OOM.

[00:03:14] Tom Nguyen: Are those at the Redwood layer or do we need to build custom middleware?

[00:03:18] Luis Ortega: Mostly in the Redwood runtime — we expose RBAC and per-tenant quotas, but you can also implement additional rate-limiters upstream. For Dedicated you can map tenants to reserved GPU pools for stronger isolation.

[00:03:29] Priya Patel: What's the recommended approach for failover? If Dedicated in region A is saturated, can we fallback to Hosted in region B without data residency violation?

[00:03:36] Maya Chen: You can configure routing policies: fallback to a compatible model variant in the same region or route to hosted with encryption and differential logging controls. For strict data residency we recommend multi-region Dedicated capacity or Private deployment. We'll outline a fallback policy with allowed fallbacks per tenant so you can enforce residency and compliance.

[00:03:52] Sara Brooks: Audit logs — do we get per-token or per-request metadata? We need the request/response hash, timestamps, and consumer principal (SAML subject).

[00:03:59] Maya Chen: We emit per-request metadata with request IDs, tenant IDs, model version, latency, and cost tokens. For Private, you can push raw logs to your SIEM; for Dedicated we can stream logs with PII redaction policies.

[00:04:12] Tom Nguyen: Back to sizing: our spikes are 10x for 15 minutes a few times a week. If we keep baseline reserved and rely on burst, what's the SLA for burst capacity?

[00:04:20] Luis Ortega: Burst SLA depends on contract. For reserved Dedicated + burst add-on we can commit to X% of burst capacity with prewarming guarantees. Otherwise, best-effort bursts are subject to available capacity in the region. We'll put concrete numbers in the pricing doc.

[00:04:34] Priya Patel: We also want to test a real workload. Can you run a POC where Redwood simulates our burst pattern and measure p99 under different warmpool sizes?

[00:04:42] Maya Chen: Absolutely. Typical next step: pilot for 2–4 weeks on Dedicated with a small warmpool and simulated bursts. We'll instrument token-level traces and produce a report. Luis can run a topology and an expected cost delta for prewarm vs over-reserve.

[00:04:56] Tom Nguyen: What's the onboarding time to Dedicated? We need it to be under 2 weeks for a pilot.

[00:05:00] Maya Chen: For standard Dedicated it's about 3–10 business days to provision in most regions, depends on GPU availability. For faster access we have an expedited path for pilots — I'll include that in the pricing email.

[00:05:09] Sara Brooks: Security question — can we use our HSM KMS, or do we need to use Redwood's?

[00:05:14] Luis Ortega: We support customer-managed keys via KMS connectors (AWS KMS, Azure, GCP) and can integrate with HSMs on Private. For Dedicated, we can do envelope encryption where CMK wraps service keys; HSM direct attachment typically requires Private.

[00:05:28] Priya Patel: Any constraints on model versions — we plan to use an in-house fine-tuned model and may want to run it on Dedicated.

[00:05:34] Maya Chen: You can bring-your-own-model (BYOM) to Dedicated. We'll need the model artifacts and a quick onboarding run to validate memory/latency. For large models we'll suggest quantization and memory-optimized kernels. We'll flag compatibility issues during onboarding.

[00:05:46] Tom Nguyen: If we bring a finetuned model that uses a custom attention op, are we blocked?

[00:05:51] Luis Ortega: Rare ops may require custom kernels; we have a path for engineering to validate and, if required, compile a runtime variant. That adds time — we'll scope that if you share the model profile.

[00:06:00] Priya Patel: Sounds good. A couple small items: cost allocation per team, tagging, and multi-tenant billing.

[00:06:06] Maya Chen: We have token-level chargeback exported per tenant and tagging support. For Dedicated, you can have multiple projects with quotas and per-project reports.

[00:06:14] Tom Nguyen: Ok, let's do the concrete next steps.

[00:06:16] Maya Chen: Recap: we'll send Dedicated pricing matrix and explicit burst SLA options, Luis will produce a topology sketch with hot/warmpool sizing and prewarm timing estimates, and we'll propose a 2-week pilot with instrumentation. Customer will share qps histogram and any model artifacts for validation.

[00:06:29] Priya Patel: Perfect. For the pilot, can you also include an example fallback policy that routes to hosted but strips embeddings for EU tenants?

[00:06:36] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll include a fallback policy template that includes per-tenant allowed fallbacks and redaction rules.

[00:06:41] Sara Brooks: And please include the SOC2 and ISO docs in the security packet.

[00:06:44] Maya Chen: Will do. Anything else?

[00:06:47] Tom Nguyen: Not from me.

[00:06:49] Priya Patel: That's it. Thanks.

[00:06:52] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the items we listed.

[00:07:00] End of recording (call continues off-record with pricing chat)

Notes on transcription errors: multiple instances where KV cache was transcribed as K V cash or K V cash, Redwood Dedicated sometimes shows as Redwood Dedicate in auto text. Occasionally speaker labels collapsed to Speaker 1 in the raw export.
